title: 1.1 Sources and conventions
text: MCF-stack collects special solutions of mean curvature flow in four categories: self-shrinkers, translators, self-expanders, and other special flows. This introduction and those four categories form the reading collection. Each example records its equation or construction, source-supported geometric properties, and a picture. Remark 1.1.1 (The source editions) . 912105D5B712 References identify the original papers or the exact supplied editions. Citations distinguish printed page numbers from PDF page numbers and retain original theorem numbers. The source inventory records file hashes and which passages have been checked; an inventoried paper has not necessarily been read. Original PDFs and extracted text are not redistributed. Construction and classification results cited from the literature retain external proofs unless a calculation is supplied here. Remark 1.1.2 (Mean curvature flow and normalization) . 4EDA6AEDEA07 For a smooth immersion $X:M^ n\times I\to \mathbb R^ N$, mean curvature flow is the geometric equation \[  (\partial _ tX)^\perp =\vec H,  \] where $\vec H$ is the trace of the second fundamental form and $\perp $ means normal projection. For hypersurfaces we use $H=\operatorname {div}_ M\nu $ and $\vec H=-H\nu $. Thus the outward normal of a round sphere has positive scalar mean curvature, and the sphere shrinks. For a smooth closed evolving submanifold, \[  \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname {Area}(M_ t)=-\int _{M_ t}|\vec H|^2\, d\mu _ t.  \] Our self-shrinkers satisfy $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ and generate $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. Self-expanders satisfy $\vec H=X^\perp /2$ and generate $M_ t=\sqrt t\, \Sigma $ for $t>0$. A translator satisfies $\vec H=V^\perp $ for a constant velocity $V$, with $M_ t=\Sigma +tV$. The translator pictures use upward unit speed unless stated otherwise. Dimensions, domains, scales, and time intervals are specified in each entry. Remark 1.1.3 (Scope and illustrations) . 57833B199F67 The first selection contains 31 examples: 10 shrinkers, 11 translators, 6 expanders, and 4 other special flows. The last category includes stationary solutions, ancient solutions, and other distinguished evolutions. Ancient means defined for all $t<T$ for some finite $T$; eternal means defined for all real times. Neither condition implies that the solution is a soliton. Explicit formulas are distinguished from implicit equations, ODE constructions, and asymptotic profiles. Every example has a figure. Interactive three-dimensional models allow rotation and zoom; higher-dimensional examples use projections, profiles, or schematics. Captions distinguish exact geometry, numerical ODE approximations, and schematic drawings, and identify truncated noncompact ends. These pictures do not replace the cited existence results. The collection is a growing reference, not an exhaustive classification or a formally verified library.

title: 2.1 Round shrinking spheres
text: Throughout this collection, the normalized self-shrinker equation is $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and a normalized shrinker $\Sigma $ generates $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $, $-\infty <t<0$. The standard examples appear in [ CM12 ] , pp. 757–759, and [ CatDLN2018 ] , Section 3.3, PDF p. 8. Example 2.1.1 (Round shrinking spheres) . 5D6AFC4ECF1B For an integer $n\geq 1$, an extinction time $T\in \mathbb R$, and a center $a\in \mathbb R^{n+1}$, the exact family is \[  M_ t=\{ a+\sqrt{2n(T-t)}\, \omega :\omega \in S^ n(1)\} , \qquad -\infty <t<T.  \] The centered normalized slice is $S^ n(\sqrt{2n})$ at $t=-1$. These are smooth compact embedded hypersurfaces without boundary, complete and proper, with topology $S^ n$ and full rotational symmetry. The case $n=1$ is the shrinking circle in the plane. With outward normal and $H=\operatorname {div}\nu $, all principal curvatures are $1/\sqrt{2n(T-t)}$. Thus the flow is strictly convex, $H=\sqrt{n/(2(T-t))}$ and $|A|^2=1/(2(T-t))$. It becomes extinct at $a$ in a Type I singularity at time $T$. The round sphere is entropy stable and $F$-stable, where $F$-stability allows the Gaussian center and scale to vary. These are the stability notions in [ CM12 ] , Theorems 0.12 and 0.16; stability of Gaussian area with center and scale fixed is a different question. The normalized Gaussian integral gives \[  \lambda (S^ n(\sqrt{2n})) =(4\pi )^{-n/2}(2n)^{n/2}e^{-n/2}|S^ n(1)|.  \] In particular, a two-sphere has entropy $4/e$. The three-dimensional picture is the exact surface for $n=2$; for other dimensions a round profile represents the symmetry reduction.

title: 2.2 Generalized shrinking cylinders
text: The cylinder family is recorded in [ CM12 ] , pp. 758–759. The spherical factor and the number of Euclidean directions are independent discrete parameters. Example 2.2.1 (Generalized shrinking cylinders) . D20709465D01 Let $n\geq 2$ and $1\leq k<n$. In $\mathbb R^{k+1}\times \mathbb R^{n-k}=\mathbb R^{n+1}$ the exact flow is \[  M_ t=S^ k(\sqrt{2k(-t)})\times \mathbb R^{n-k},\qquad -\infty <t<0.  \] Equivalently, $(\omega ,z)\mapsto (\sqrt{2k(-t)}\, \omega ,z)$, with $\omega \in S^ k(1)$ and $z\in \mathbb R^{n-k}$, is a normal parametrization of the flow. These are complete, proper, noncompact embedded hypersurfaces without boundary, with topology $S^ k\times \mathbb R^{n-k}$ and polynomial area growth. Their symmetries include $O(k+1)$ on the spherical factor and all Euclidean isometries in the axial factor. There are $k$ positive principal curvatures $1/\sqrt{2k(-t)}$ and $n-k$ zero principal curvatures. Hence they are mean convex and weakly convex, and $|A|^2=1/(2(-t))$. At time zero the spherical factor collapses onto the axial subspace. Topologically there are two ends if $n-k=1$, and one end if $n-k\geq 2$. Each end has exactly the displayed product geometry. They are entropy stable among the complete embedded hypersurfaces considered by [ CM12 ] , but are not $F$-stable when $1\leq k<n$; see Theorems 0.12 and 0.16. The Euclidean factor leaves entropy unchanged: $\lambda (M_{-1})=\lambda (S^ k(\sqrt{2k}))$. For the round cylinder in $\mathbb R^3$, this is $\sqrt{2\pi /e}$. For $n=2$, $k=1$, an interactive picture displays an exact finite window of the infinite cylinder. End caps are not part of the solution.

title: 2.3 Planes through the shrinker center
text: Planes are stationary solutions that also satisfy the shrinker equation; see [ CatDLN2018 ] , Sections 2.5 and 3.3, and [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.16. Example 2.3.1 (Planes through the shrinker center) . 97FD822B6630 Let $P$ be an $n$-dimensional linear subspace of $\mathbb R^ N$, where $1\leq n<N$. Then \[  M_ t=P,\qquad -\infty <t<\infty , \qquad \vec H=0,\quad X^\perp =0.  \] Thus $P$ is both a stationary flow and a normalized self-shrinker. An affine plane is a shrinker centered at any point of that plane; it satisfies the centered equation at the origin only if it contains the origin. The inclusion is complete, proper, embedded, flat, noncompact and boundaryless, with topology $\mathbb R^ n$ and Euclidean volume growth. It has two ends for $n=1$ and one end for $n\geq 2$. The solution has no finite singular time. The identity $\sqrt{-t}\, P=P$ does not describe a geometric collapse. Its entropy is exactly one. In codimension one it is entropy stable and $F$-stable under the notions in [ CM12 ] ; no conclusion about a different constrained variation problem is intended. The picture shows a bounded patch of a plane in $\mathbb R^3$. Its boundary is a viewing boundary, not a boundary of the flow.

title: 2.4 Abresch–Langer closed shrinking curves
text: The closed planar curves are classified by [ CatAL1986 ] . The supplied sources record the curvature conservation laws in [ CatDLN2018 ] , Theorem 1, PDF pp. 5–6, and the rotation-index description in [ CatCMComplexity2020 ] , Section 6.3, supplied PDF p. 22. Example 2.4.1 (Abresch–Langer closed shrinking curves) . 55D5743A6941 Besides the round circle, there are noncircular closed immersed curves $\gamma _{m,\ell }\subset \mathbb R^2$, indexed primitively by coprime positive integers satisfying \[  \frac12<\frac m\ell <\frac1{\sqrt2}.  \] Here $m$ is the rotation index and $\ell $ is the number of periods of the curvature. Their flows are $\sqrt{-t}\, \gamma _{m,\ell }$ for $t<0$. An ODE description in the normalization of this collection is \[  \kappa _{\theta \theta }+\kappa =\frac1{2\kappa },\qquad \kappa >0,\qquad \kappa _\theta ^2+\kappa ^2-\log \kappa =E.  \] Choose the nonconstant periodic solution with curvature period $2\pi m/\ell $. With $T(\theta )=(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta )$ and $N(\theta )=(-\sin \theta ,\cos \theta )$, reconstruction gives \[  X(\theta )=2\kappa _\theta T(\theta )-2\kappa N(\theta ), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/(2\pi m\mathbb Z).  \] This is an ODE construction with a closing condition, not a closed elementary formula for $\kappa $. The domain is $S^1$. These are compact, complete, proper immersions with self-intersections. Their curvature is positive after orienting the curve, so they are locally strictly convex; their images do not bound convex embedded domains. The round circle is the only embedded closed shrinking curve. The noncircular curves have finite entropy strictly greater than two, as recorded in [ CatCMComplexity2020 ] , Section 6.3. The conservation law $\kappa e^{-|X|^2/4}=C>0$ relates curvature to distance from the shrinking center. Compactness makes the shrinking flow a Type I flow becoming extinct at the origin. The figure shows the numerical closed profile with $(m,\ell )=(2,3)$. Its caption records the closure residual.

title: 2.5 Angenent's shrinking torus
text: Angenent constructs an embedded rotational self-shrinker with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$ for each $n\geq 2$ in [ CatAngenent1992 ] . We use the normalized profile equation from [ CatDLN2018 ] , Section 3.3 and equation (5.2), PDF pp. 8 and 14. Example 2.5.1 (Angenent's shrinking torus) . 10374A017921 There is a simple closed profile $s\mapsto (x(s),r(s))$ in $r>0$ whose rotation gives \[  X(s,\omega )=(x(s),r(s)\omega )\in \mathbb R\times \mathbb R^ n, \qquad \omega \in S^{n-1}(1).  \] For Euclidean arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $, the profile solves \[  x'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad r'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\left(\frac{n-1}{r}-\frac r2\right)\cos \alpha +\frac x2\sin \alpha .  \] Equivalently, it is a closed geodesic of $r^{2(n-1)}e^{-(x^2+r^2)/2}(dx^2+dr^2)$ on $r>0$. The theorem selects a closed orbit by shooting; the profile is not given by a closed formula. Its flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $, $t<0$. The hypersurface is compact, embedded, complete and proper, with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$, rotational $O(n)$ symmetry and reflection symmetry across $x=0$. When $n=2$ it is a torus in $\mathbb R^3$. It is not mean convex. Indeed, the compact embedded mean-convex classification in [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.17, would force a sphere. It shrinks to the origin with a Type I singularity. It is entropy unstable by [ CM12 ] , Theorem 0.12, which applies to this compact embedded non-spherical hypersurface. No explicit entropy value or global uniqueness assertion is supplied here. The interactive figure revolves a numerically closed solution of this ODE; its caption records the shooting residual. The profile is not circular. The variational torus in [ CatDLN2018 ] , Theorem 2, is a separate existence construction; that survey does not identify it with Angenent's torus.

title: 2.6 Drugan's immersed shrinking spheres
text: [ CatDrugan2015 ] , Theorem 1.1, p. 3139, proves the existence of a nonembedded immersed $S^2$ self-shrinker in $\mathbb R^3$. [ CatDLN2018 ] , Theorem 3, PDF pp. 14–15, gives the corresponding existence statement for $S^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\geq 2$. Example 2.6.1 (Drugan's immersed shrinking spheres) . FE38A115C52C For each $n\geq 2$, there is a smooth rotational immersion $X:S^ n\to \mathbb R^{n+1}$ satisfying $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ whose image is not embedded. The associated immersed flow is $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$, $-\infty <t<0$. In the three-dimensional construction, a graphical piece of the profile, written as axial height $z=\gamma (r)$ for $r>0$, solves \[  \frac{\gamma ''}{1+(\gamma ')^2} =\left(\frac r2-\frac1r\right)\gamma '-\frac\gamma 2.  \] This is equation (1.3) of [ CatDrugan2015 ] , p. 3140. Shooting and continuation through profile turning points produce the closed immersed sphere; a single graphical piece does not describe the whole surface. The parameter domain is the compact sphere, so the induced metric is complete and the immersion is proper. The image has self-intersections and is not the round sphere. The construction has rotational symmetry and reflection symmetry across a hyperplane perpendicular to the rotation axis. It has no ends. The homothetic flow contracts to the origin with Type I curvature growth. The cited existence argument supplies neither an elementary parametrization nor uniqueness or an exact entropy value. Embedded classification and embedded stability theorems cannot be applied to this immersion by dropping their embeddedness hypothesis. The numerical profile in [ CatDrugan2015 ] , Figure 1, is an illustration of the shooting construction. Our diagram records the domain topology and the distinction between immersion and embedding; it does not solve the shooting problem.

section: 2.7 The Clifford shrinking torus in four-space
text: We follow the supplied June 2020 version of [ CatELS2020 ] ; its Sections 2, 4 and 5 distinguish exact geometry, Hamiltonian stability, flow instability and local rigidity. Example 2.7.1 (The Clifford shrinking torus in four-space) . 635FBEF68A7E The exact normalized immersion is \[  X(\theta _1,\theta _2)=\sqrt2 (\cos \theta _1,\sin \theta _1,\cos \theta _2,\sin \theta _2), \qquad (\theta _1,\theta _2)\in (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2.  \] It lies in $\mathbb R^4=\mathbb C^2$, and $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ gives a smooth flow for $t<0$. This is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus of dimension two and codimension two, complete and proper. It is minimal in $S^3(2)$ and has the product rotation symmetry $U(1)\times U(1)$. The induced metric is $2(d\theta _1^2+d\theta _2^2)$; it is intrinsically flat, has area $8\pi ^2$, $|\vec H|=1$, and $\vec H=-X/2$. Its entropy is exactly $2\pi /e$ ( [ CatELS2020 ] , Section 2 and Lemma 2.4, PDF pp. 3–6). It is $F$-unstable under Lagrangian variations but $F$-stable under Hamiltonian variations after accounting for translations. It is locally volume minimizing under Hamiltonian variations (Lemmas 4.1–4.2 and Theorem 4.3, PDF p. 13). Nevertheless it is not a local entropy minimum, even within Hamiltonian variations. For every $\varepsilon >0$ and $k\in \mathbb N$ there is a compact embedded Lagrangian torus Hamiltonian isotopic and $\varepsilon $-close in $C^ k$ whose first finite-time singularity has a blow-up outside the $U(2)$-orbit of the Clifford torus (Corollary 4.8 and Theorem 4.9, PDF p. 16). A compact embedded two-dimensional self-shrinker in $\mathbb C^2$ sufficiently $C^{2,\alpha }$-close, for $0<\alpha <1$, is the Clifford torus up to translation, dilation and rotation (Theorem 5.7, PDF p. 29). This is a local rigidity statement. The interactive picture rotates the second and fourth coordinates in $\mathbb R^4$ and then projects onto the first three coordinates. Apparent intersections in a projection do not mean that the original torus is immersed nonembedded.

title: 2.8 Products of closed shrinking curves
text: [ CatSmoczyk2005 ] , equation (1.4), p. 2984, describes these Lagrangian products. That paper uses $\vec H=-X^\perp $; spatial dilation by $\sqrt2$ converts its examples to the convention used here. Example 2.8.1 (Products of closed shrinking curves) . AD717A30B415 Let $m\geq 2$ and let each $\gamma _ j:S^1\to \mathbb R^2$ be a normalized closed Abresch–Langer shrinker, including the round circle if desired. Then \[  X(u_1,\ldots ,u_ m) =(\gamma _1(u_1),\ldots ,\gamma _ m(u_ m))\in \mathbb R^{2m}, \qquad (u_1,\ldots ,u_ m)\in (S^1)^ m  \] satisfies $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and $X_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X$ for $t<0$. The product formula is exact, but any noncircular factor still requires the curvature ODE and closing condition. The domain is the compact $m$-torus. These are complete proper immersions of dimension and codimension $m$, Lagrangian in $\mathbb C^ m$, with flat normal bundle and nowhere vanishing mean-curvature vector. The product metric is intrinsically flat. A product is embedded when every factor is an embedded circle. A noncircular factor has self-intersections, and so does the product immersion. Multiple covers must not be treated as embeddings. Unless all factor images are circles, the image is not contained in a sphere. The all-circle product in $\mathbb R^4$ is the Clifford torus described separately above. These compact products have no ends, finite entropy and a Type I homothetic extinction at the origin. No general stability or uniqueness claim for this family is taken from the cited product construction. The figure displays the planar factors and identifies the ambient dimension of their product.

title: 2.9 Higher-codimension spherical shrinkers
text: Minimal submanifolds of a round sphere give Euclidean self-shrinkers. This correspondence, and a converse with hypotheses, appear in [ CatSmoczyk2005 ] , p. 2985 and Theorem 1.1. We use the $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ scaling. Example 2.9.1 (Higher-codimension spherical shrinkers) . 45597E4891F4 Let $n\geq 2$ and let $F:M^ n\to S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$ be a smooth compact minimal immersion. Viewed in $\mathbb R^ N$, it satisfies \[  \vec H=-\frac12F, \qquad F_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, F,\quad -\infty <t<0.  \] An explicit family is obtained for integers $p,q\geq 1$, $n=p+q$, by \[  F(u,v)=(\sqrt{2p}\, u,\sqrt{2q}\, v), \quad (u,v)\in S^ p(1)\times S^ q(1), \quad N=p+q+2.  \] To avoid repeating the Clifford torus entry, one may take $p+q\geq 3$ in this explicit family. For a general compact minimal immersion, the resulting shrinker is complete and proper; it is embedded when the original immersion is embedded. Topology, symmetry and further curvature properties depend on the chosen minimal submanifold and are not fixed by this construction. Its mean-curvature vector has constant length $\sqrt{n/2}$, and the principal normal $\vec H/|\vec H|$ is parallel in the normal bundle. Conversely, a compact self-shrinker of dimension $n\geq 2$ is spherical if and only if its mean-curvature vector is nowhere zero and its principal normal is parallel (Smoczyk's Theorem 1.1). The displayed product family is compact embedded of Euclidean codimension two, with topology $S^ p\times S^ q$ and $O(p+1)\times O(q+1)$ symmetry. It has $|A|^2=1$ and is minimal inside $S^{n+1}(\sqrt{2n})$; these identities follow directly from its two round factors. The formula determines the product geometry exactly. The figure is a factor diagram with the full ambient dimension stated.

section: 2.10 Moller closed shrinkers of large even genus
text: Møller's construction is stated in [ CatMoller2014 ] , Theorem 1, and summarized in the supplied [ CatDLN2018 ] , Section 3.3, PDF pp. 10–11. Example 2.10.1 (Moller closed shrinkers of large even genus) . A105C87CB202 There is an integer $g_0$ such that for every even $g\geq g_0$ there exists a compact smooth embedded orientable surface $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ satisfying $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$. Its flow is $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$, $t<0$. This is an existence construction by desingularization, not an explicit formula and not an existence assertion for every positive genus. Each surface is complete and proper, has no ends, and is invariant under a dihedral group of order $2g$. Along the constructed family as $g\to \infty $, the surfaces converge in Hausdorff distance to the union of a round shrinking sphere and a rotational shrinking torus. Convergence is locally smooth away from their two intersection circles ( [ CatMoller2014 ] , pp. 1–2). The limiting union is singular and is not one of the smooth members. These surfaces are not mean convex and are entropy unstable: apply [ CM12 ] , Theorems 0.17 and 0.12, to the compact embedded non-spherical surfaces. Their homothetic flows have Type I extinction at the origin. The cited construction supplies no exact coordinates or exact entropy value and makes no uniqueness assertion for a specified genus. The figure shows the limiting sphere–torus configuration and its intersection circles. It illustrates the input to the desingularization, not the constructed surface $\Sigma _ g$.

title: 3.1 The grim reaper and its cylinders

section: 3.1 The grim reaper and its cylinders
text: Example 3.1.1 (The grim reaper and its cylinders) . 3B1939BC4D74 For unit upward translation, an exact parametrization in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=(x,y,-\log \cos x+t),\qquad |x|<\pi /2,\quad y\in \mathbb R^{n-1},\quad t\in \mathbb R.  \] For $n=1$ omit $y$. More generally the planar curve of speed $c>0$ has height $-c^{-1}\log \cos (cx)+ct$, on $|x|<\pi /(2c)$. The curve and all its Euclidean products are complete, properly embedded, noncompact, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. Their motion is eternal. At unit speed the curve has curvature magnitude $\cos x$ and total curvature $\pi $. Its two ends have the vertical asymptotes $x=\pm \pi /2$. The product is invariant under translations in its $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ factor. For $n\geq 2$ its second fundamental form has rank one; in $\mathbb R^3$ its Gauss curvature is zero, so it is not strictly convex. As a translating graph it is stable for compactly supported variations of the translator weighted area. This is weighted stability, not a claim about stability for unweighted Euclidean area. The supplied notes [ CatHIMWNotes19 ] , Example 1.6, PDF page 4, use downward translation; the displayed surface is its reflection in a horizontal plane. Graphical weighted minimality is discussed in [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , Section 2, PDF page 5.

title: 3.2 Tilted grim-reaper cylinders
text: Example 3.2.1 (Tilted grim-reaper cylinders) . 56A3E33A9D04 Let $a\in \mathbb R$ and $A=1+a^2$. An exact unit-speed upward translator in $\mathbb R^3$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=\left(x,y,-A\log \cos (x/\sqrt A)+ay+t\right),\quad |x|<\frac\pi 2\sqrt A,\quad y,t\in \mathbb R.  \] This is a complete, properly embedded noncompact surface diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$. It has zero Gauss curvature and is invariant under translation in the direction $(0,1,a)$. Its horizontal graph domain is a strip of width $\pi \sqrt{1+a^2}$. The case $a=0$ is the ordinary grim-reaper cylinder. The underlying surface is a rotation and dilation of that cylinder. At a fixed width greater than $\pi $, the two signs of $a$ give the two opposite tilts. Translation in a tangent invariant direction does not change the evolving image. Products with Euclidean factors give higher-dimensional translators. Graphical weighted stability holds, as in the preceding example. See [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , equation (1.4), PDF page 3, with exchanged horizontal coordinates and reflected vertical direction. These cylinders must be distinguished from the strictly convex $\Delta $-wings on strips of the same width.

title: 3.3 The rotational bowl translator
text: Example 3.3.1 (The rotational bowl translator) . ECF360A3D482 For each $n\geq 2$, the bowl is the entire graph $z=f(r)$, $r=|x|$ in $\mathbb R^ n$, moving by $z\mapsto z+t$. Its radial profile is specified by the regular ODE \[  \frac{f''}{1+(f')^2}+\frac{n-1}{r}f'=1,\qquad f(0)=f'(0)=0,\qquad f''(0)=1/n.  \] This is an ODE characterization, not an elementary closed formula. The bowl is complete, properly embedded, strictly convex, rotationally invariant, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. For $n\geq 2$ it has one topological end and gives an eternal flow. Up to a vertical additive constant, its height has asymptotic expansion \[  f(r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C+O(r^{-1})\quad (r\to \infty ).  \] A paraboloid is only a leading approximation, not the exact translator. It is unique among entire rotationally invariant translating graphs, up to translation. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is the only complete entire translating graph, up to the natural rigid motions and normalization. In $\mathbb R^3$, Brendle–Choi's theorem characterizes its flow among noncompact, strictly convex, noncollapsed ancient flows, up to scaling and ambient isometries. These are the hypotheses of the cited classification. Graphical weighted stability holds. The stronger dynamical stability theorem of Clutterbuck–Schnürer–Schulze concerns continuous graphical initial data whose height difference from the bowl tends to zero at spatial infinity; the resulting height difference tends uniformly to zero as time tends to infinity. The supplied notes [ CatHIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4 and Theorem 4.1, PDF pages 10–11, describe the construction and classification. The original ODE and asymptotic analysis is [ CSS07 ] , Section 2, Lemmas 2.1–2.2; its Theorem 1.1 gives the stated dynamical stability. The ancient classification is [ CatBrendleChoi19 ] , Theorem 1.1, printed page 36 (PDF page 2).

title: 3.4 Rotational translating catenoids
text: Example 3.4.1 (Rotational translating catenoids) . 72E3A9DEA98C For every neck radius $R>0$ and $n\geq 2$, there is a rotational translating hypersurface with two ends. These are also called winglike translators. They move upward with unit speed. A convenient numerical description uses meridian arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $: \[  r'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad z'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\cos \alpha -\frac{n-1}{r}\sin \alpha , \qquad (r,z,\alpha )(0)=(R,0,\pi /2).  \] Revolution gives $(r(s)\omega ,z(s)+t)$ with $\omega \in S^{n-1}$ and $t\in \mathbb R$. The arclength system is obtained from $\vec H=e_{n+1}^{\perp }$ and is not a closed formula. The surface is complete, embedded, noncompact and nonconvex, with topology $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is an annulus, not an entire graph. Outside the neck the two ends are radial graphs. Each has expansion \[  f_\pm (r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C_\pm +O(r^{-1}).  \] In particular the two ends go to spatial infinity and the complete surface is proper. The parameter controls the neck radius. The supplied survey describes the limiting double bowl with a singular point on the axis as the neck parameter tends to zero. See [ CatHIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4, PDF page 10. The original construction and end expansion are [ CSS07 ] , Lemma 2.3, PDF pages 5–7 of the author preprint. No uniqueness beyond the radial initial-value construction, nor an entropy or stability classification for this non-graphical surface, is asserted here.

title: 3.5 Strictly convex delta-wing translators
text: Example 3.5.1 (Strictly convex delta-wing translators) . B72E7DC6B42E For every $b>\pi /2$, there is a complete strictly convex unit-speed translator that is a graph $z=u_ b(x,y)$ over \[  (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times (-b,b),\qquad \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{(u_ b)_ i(u_ b)_ j}{1+|Du_ b|^2}\right)(u_ b)_{ij}=1.  \] This is a nonlinear PDE characterization; no explicit height formula is supplied. The graph is embedded, noncompact, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$, and has positive Gauss curvature everywhere. After centering and a vertical translation, $u_ b(0,0)=0$ is its minimum and $u_ b$ is even in both coordinates. The width is exactly $2b>\pi $. Among complete translators on this strip that are not tilted grim reapers, it is unique up to translation. The centered solution depends smoothly on compact sets under limits of the width parameter. Along the two unbounded horizontal directions, translated graphs converge smoothly to the two oppositely tilted grim-reaper cylinders of the same strip width. Their angle is determined by \[  \cos \theta =\frac{\pi }{2b}.  \] This relation follows from the explicit tilted-cylinder width; the supplied preprint has an inverted ratio in its printed statement of Theorem 2.4. Graphical weighted stability holds. This is a strictly convex surface, whereas the tilted grim-reaper cylinders on the same strip have zero Gauss curvature. See [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorems 1.1, 2.4, 4.1 and 5.7 and Corollary 5.5 (PDF pages 4, 6, 10–12). The construction, uniqueness, and asymptotic results are cited rather than reproduced here. An illustration of the strip and its two limiting grim cylinders is a schematic of its asymptotics, not a computed solution $u_ b$.

title: 3.6 Nonrotational entire convex translators
text: Example 3.6.1 (Nonrotational entire convex translators) . 0F00F9295CD9 In every dimension $n\geq 3$, Xu-Jia Wang constructs entire convex solutions $u:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ of the unit-speed upward translator equation \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}\right)u_{ij}=1  \] whose level sets are not spheres or round cylinders in any orthogonal coordinate system. This is an existence construction, not an explicit formula. The graphs are embedded, complete, proper and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$; the last three facts also follow directly from being smooth entire graphs. Their flows exist for all $t\in \mathbb R$ by translation. They are convex and break the spherical or cylindrical rotational pattern of the bowl and its Euclidean products. The corresponding statement for complete entire graphs in $\mathbb R^3$ is false: there the bowl is the only example. Under spatial blow-down $u_ h(x)=h^{-1}u(\sqrt h\, x)$, Wang's theorem gives, after rotations depending on $h$, a quadratic limit of the form \[  \frac{x_1^2+\cdots +x_ k^2}{2(k-1)},\qquad 2\leq k\leq n.  \] The theorem does not rule out slow rotation of the axes as $h\to \infty $. This is an asymptotic limit, not a formula for $u$. The same paper also constructs nonrotational complete convex graphical translators over slab regions. No uniqueness theorem for the general higher-dimensional families is claimed here. See [ CatXJWang11 ] , Theorems 1.2–1.3, printed pages 1187–1188 (PDF pages 3–4), using the case $\sigma =1$ of equation (1.2); the $\sigma =0$ case describes a different, level-set formulation. title: 3.7 Translators with prescribed apex curvatures
text: Example 3.7.1 (Translators with prescribed apex curvatures) . D68656E88625 Let $k_1,\ldots ,k_ n\geq 0$ with $\sum _ i k_ i=1$. Hoffman–Ilmanen–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded translating graph over an open domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$. After reflecting their downward convention to upward translation, it satisfies \[  \min u=u(0)=0,\qquad D^2u(0)=\operatorname {diag}(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n).  \] These equations specify apex data, not an explicit global formula. The function is even in every coordinate. If $k_ i=0$ it is invariant under translation in the $i$-th coordinate; if $k_ i>0$, then $D_ i u$ has the same sign as $x_ i$ away from $x_ i=0$. Equal apex curvatures $k_ i=k_ j$ give invariance under rotations in the $(x_ i,x_ j)$-plane. The domain is either all of $\mathbb R^ n$ or a slab $\{ |x_ i|<b\} $. In the slab case the corresponding $k_ i$ is strictly larger than every other $k_ j$. If the two largest prescribed curvatures are equal, the resulting graph is entire. The supplied edition obtains an $(n-2)$-parameter family of pairwise noncongruent entire examples this way. The construction gives existence and the listed symmetries, but does not assert general uniqueness or convexity of every higher-dimensional graph. In particular, apex positivity alone is not a global convexity theorem. See [ CatHIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2, PDF page 18. title: 3.9 The pitchfork translator

title: 4.1 Expanding smoothings of planar corners
text: The convention throughout these entries is $\vec H=X^\perp /2$ for the time-one profile. Thus $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M$, $t>0$, is the corresponding flow. The positive weight for variational statements is $e^{|X|^2/4}$; minimizing this weighted area locally will be called $E$-minimizing. Example 4.1.1 (Even graphical corner expanders) . 72808FA576A9 For every $\kappa >0$ there is a smooth even function $\phi _\kappa :\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ satisfying \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{x\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{|x|\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (x)}{|x|}=\kappa .  \] The profile $\Gamma _\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (x)):x\in \mathbb R\} $ is a smooth complete properly embedded noncompact curve in $\mathbb R^2$, with topology $\mathbb R$, reflection symmetry, and two ends asymptotic to the rays of $y=\kappa |x|$. It is $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. Its curvature vector is nonzero and points along the upward graph normal: writing $q=\phi _\kappa -x\phi _\kappa '$ gives $q'=-x(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$ and $\phi _\kappa ''=(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$, with $q(0)>0$. The source gives the quantitative estimate, for $x>0$, \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (x)-\kappa x \leq \min \left\{ \frac{2e(\kappa +2)}{x}e^{-x^2/4},\, 3\kappa +2\right\} .  \] The flow $\sqrt t\, \Gamma _\kappa $, $t\in (0,\infty )$, smooths the corner at time zero. These are ODE-defined profiles, not elementary closed formulas. Source: [ CatDing20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.9)–(4.15), printed pp. 373–374, supplied PDF pp. 15–16. The figure shows a numerical ODE profile with $\phi (0)=1$. Taking the product with $\mathbb R$ gives an example in $\mathbb R^3$ with one zero principal curvature.

text: Example 4.2.1 (Entire radial cone smoothings) . D3CC5E948716 For $n\geq 2$ and $\kappa >0$, consider \[  M_\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} \subset \mathbb R^{n+1},  \] where $\phi _\kappa $ is the smooth radial solution constructed with \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{n-1}{r}\phi _\kappa ' +\frac{r\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{r\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (r)}r=\kappa .  \] The equation at $r=0$ is interpreted by smooth radial extension; it implies $\phi _\kappa ''(0)=\phi _\kappa (0)/(2n)$. The hypersurface is smooth, complete, properly embedded, noncompact, rotationally symmetric, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$, and $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. It has one conical end and nondecreasing height. The estimate \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (r)-\kappa r \leq ((n+1)\kappa +2)\min \{ 1,r^{-1}\} ,\qquad r>0,  \] records the rate at which it approaches its cone. Its flow is $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M_\kappa $ for $t>0$, with initial cone $z=\kappa |x|$. Source: [ CatDing20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.1), (4.7), and (4.8), printed pp. 371–373, supplied PDF pp. 13–15. section: 4.3 Two-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
text: Example 4.3.1 (Disconnected double-cone smoothings) . 4F35D93CA4BD Let $n\geq 2$, write $(x,z)\in \mathbb R^ n\times \mathbb R$, and let \[  D_\alpha =\{ (x,z):|x|=|z|\tan \alpha \} ,\qquad 0<\alpha <\pi /2.  \] With $\phi _{\cot \alpha }$ from Example 4.2.1 , the two-sheeted expander is \[  M_\alpha ^{(2)} =\{ (x,\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\}  \mathbin {\cup } \{ (x,-\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} .  \] This display specifies the surface using ODE-defined functions. Its two components are smooth, complete, properly embedded convex entire graphs, each diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. The union is noncompact, invariant under rotations about the $z$-axis and under $z\mapsto -z$, and has two oppositely directed conical ends. The flow $\sqrt t\, M_\alpha ^{(2)}$, $t>0$, approaches $D_\alpha $ as $t\downarrow 0$. Existence and uniqueness of each rotational single-lobe graphical profile are established in [ CatAIC95 ] , Lemma 2(i), printed p. 1947, supplied PDF p. 12. Theorem 4, printed pp. 1950–1951, PDF pp. 15–16, provides a critical angle $\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)\in (0,\pi /2)$. For $\alpha <\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)$ the level-set flow of the double cone is exactly the two-sheeted flow. For angles above this threshold there are also connected smoothings, so the graphical uniqueness statement does not assert uniqueness among all flows from the cone. The critical-angle decimal estimates later in that paper are numerical. The $n=2$ figure rotates two reflected numerical profiles; the cone is their asymptotic limit.

title: 4.6 Self-expanding planar tree networks
text: Example 4.6.1 (Regular expanding trees with prescribed rays) . 16898F334139 A regular planar network consists of smooth branches meeting only at triple junctions, with angles $120$ degrees at every junction. A self-expanding network $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^2$ satisfies \[  \vec k=\frac{X^\perp }{2}  \] on each open branch; its time evolution is $\Sigma _ t=\sqrt t\, \Sigma $, $t>0$, with the same angle condition. It is a network flow and is not a smooth immersed curve at its junctions. For finitely many distinct prescribed rays from the origin, connected tree-like expanders provide smoothings in this network sense. Existence for three rays, including uniqueness of the tree, and existence for more rays are recalled in [ CatINS19 ] , Section 7, printed p. 70, supplied PDF p. 32, with attribution there to Schnürer–Schulze and Mazzeo–Sáez respectively. The branches can be described as geodesics for the conformal metric \[  g=e^{|X|^2/2}(dX_1^2+dX_2^2),  \] with the junction balance condition. Noncompact ends approach their assigned rays with Gaussian decay. Two regular expanders with the same asymptotic rays coincide if they are in the same topological class: the comparison deformation must retain distinct junctions and the prescribed asymptotic ends, as in the source definition. This does not assert uniqueness across different network topologies. See [ CatINS19 ] , Lemmas 4.1 and 4.3 and Theorem 4.4, printed pp. 49–51, supplied PDF pp. 11–13. The source uses $\vec k=\psi ^\perp $ and $\sqrt{2t}\, \psi $; our profile is $\Sigma =\sqrt2\, \psi $. Nontrivial networks arise from a geodesic boundary-value construction. The exact balanced special case \[  \bigcup _{j=0}^2\{ r(\cos (2\pi j/3),\sin (2\pi j/3)):r\geq 0\}   \] is the stationary $Y$ network. It illustrates the junction condition. The accompanying general tree diagram is schematic; its branches are not numerically solved.

section: 5.1 The catenoid as an eternal stationary flow
text: Example 5.1.1 (Stationary catenoid flow) . AC1C0D984A58 For $a>0$ the explicit immersion \[  X(\theta ,s,t)=a(\cosh s\cos \theta ,\cosh s\sin \theta ,s), \quad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,\quad s\in \mathbb R,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] is independent of time and has $\vec H=0$. It is therefore an eternal stationary mean curvature flow in $\mathbb R^3$. Every time slice is a complete properly embedded noncompact rotational annulus, with two ends and a waist circle of radius $a$. Its metric and curvature are \[  g=a^2\cosh ^2s(d\theta ^2+ds^2),\qquad K=-\frac1{a^2\cosh ^4s},\qquad \int K\, dA=-4\pi .  \] The metric follows by differentiation, and the conformal curvature formula gives $K$ and its integral. The complete catenoid is unstable for compactly supported area variations: for a test function $f(s)$ independent of $\theta $, its second variation is \[  Q(f,f)=2\pi \int _{\mathbb R}\bigl ((f')^2-2\operatorname {sech}^2s\, f^2\bigr )\, ds.  \] Taking $f$ equal to one on $[-R,R]$, zero outside $[-2R,2R]$, and $|f'|\leq C/R$ makes this negative for large $R$. Each open half is a minimal graph over $r>a$, with $z=\pm a\operatorname {arcosh}(r/a)$, so it is stable for compactly supported variations in that half. These are minimal-area stability assertions, not a classification of dynamical stability under MCF. The supplied source also records the catenoid in [ CatMan11 ] , Remark 4.4.7, printed p. 105, supplied PDF p. 116. The parametrization is exact and supports interactive rotation, scale selection, and a truncated height range with the omitted infinite ends stated.

section: 5.2 Mean curvature evolution of the Whitney sphere
text: Example 5.2.1 (A collapsing Lagrangian immersed sphere) . 245DFF2BED27 For $n\geq 2$, the initial Whitney immersion in $\mathbb R^{2n}=\mathbb C^ n$ is explicitly \[  F_0(x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1}) =\frac{(x_1,x_1x_{n+1},\ldots ,x_ n,x_ nx_{n+1})}{1+x_{n+1}^2}, \qquad (x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1})\in S^ n.  \] It is a compact Lagrangian immersion, of dimension and codimension $n$, with one transverse double image point at the origin coming from the two poles. It is complete and proper as an immersion of a compact domain, and it is not embedded. Its equivariance reduces the geometry to the planar initial profile \[  \gamma _0(u)=\left(\frac{\sin u}{1+\cos ^2u}, \frac{\sin u\cos u}{1+\cos ^2u}\right), \qquad u\in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z.  \] For $n\geq 2$ the profile evolution is the equivariant equation \[  (\partial _ t\gamma )^\perp =\vec k-(n-1)\frac{\gamma ^\perp }{|\gamma |^2},  \] interpreted by the smooth equivariant immersion at the double point. It is not ordinary planar curve shortening. The maximal smooth mean curvature flow $F_ t$, $t\in [0,T)$, remains Lagrangian and equivariant. It collapses to the origin in finite time, and its tangent flow there is a Lagrangian plane with multiplicity two. The Whitney sphere is not a self-similar solution. These statements are the special case stated in [ CatViana18 ] , pp. 1–3, especially the result on p. 2 and Theorem 1.3 on p. 3. The formulas above specify the initial geometry and its reduced equation, not a closed expression for $F_ t$ at positive time. The figure shows the exact initial generating profile $\gamma _0$ of this higher-codimension immersion.

title: 5.3 Rotational degenerate neckpinch solutions
text: Example 5.3.1 (Angenent–Velázquez type-II singularities) . 922034E946EB Let $n\geq 2$, let $m\geq 3$ be odd, and let $K>0$. Choose a compact rotational target hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, smooth away from a cusp at the origin, whose radius satisfies $u_*(x)\sim \sqrt K\, x^{m/2}$ as $x\downarrow 0$ and whose other tip closes smoothly. Angenent and Velázquez construct smooth compact rotational mean curvature flows \[  M_ t=\{ (x,u(x,t)\omega ):a(t)\leq x\leq b(t),\  \omega \in S^{n-1}\} , \qquad t_0<t<T,  \] with smooth caps and positive radius between them. Each regular slice is an embedded sphere, hence complete and proper. The constructed flows remain close to the chosen target outside a small neighborhood of the origin as the construction interval is shortened. They are not supplied as ancient solutions or as solitons, and no closed formula for $u(x,t)$ is given. Set $\xi _*=(2(n-1)/K)^{1/m}$. At the left tip, \[  a(t)=-(\xi _*+o(1))(T-t)^{1/m},\qquad |\vec H|_{\rm tip}(t)=\left(\frac{\xi _*}{m}+o(1)\right)(T-t)^{1/m-1}.  \] Here the curvature coefficient is for the trace mean curvature, equivalently the magnitude $|\vec H|$ at this convex tip. Rotational smoothness makes the $n$ principal curvatures equal at the tip, so $|A|_{\rm tip}=|\vec H|_{\rm tip}/\sqrt n$. The maximum of $|A|$ is attained there; its blow-up rate is type II. The parabolic rescalings at the origin converge smoothly on compact sets to $S^{n-1}_{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}\times \mathbb R$, whereas rescaling about the tip by $A_{\max }(t)=\max _{M_ t}|A|$ yields the rotational translating bowl with tip $|A|=1$. This last normalization has translation speed $\sqrt n$; rescaling instead by $|\vec H|_{\rm tip}$ gives the speed-one bowl. Under the intermediate scaling $x\mapsto x/(T-t)^{1/m}$ and $r\mapsto r/(T-t)^{1/2}$, the limiting profile is \[  r=\sqrt{2(n-1)+Kx^ m},\qquad x\geq -\xi _*.  \] This last expression is an asymptotic limiting profile, not an exact formula for the evolving compact hypersurface. Source: [ CatAV97 ] , Introduction, items 1–5, printed pp. 16–17, supplied PDF pp. 2–3; the construction is justified in Sections 3–7. The even-$m$ modifications and the formal $m=2$ discussion are not included in this entry. The figure compares the three scaling regimes: the full compact surface is schematic and the intermediate profile is a limit. The construction does not classify all type-II singularities or impose global convexity on every allowed target.

section: 5.4 The Angenent oval as an explicit ancient flow
text: Example 5.4.1 (The ancient paperclip curve) . B008243C5D96 With the speed-one curve-shortening convention, the exact implicit equation \[  \Gamma _ t=\{ (x,y)\in \mathbb R^2:|x|<\pi /2,\  e^ t\cosh y=\cos x\} , \qquad -\infty <t<0,  \] defines the Angenent oval. Equivalently, its two graph branches are \[  y=\pm \operatorname {arcosh}(e^{-t}\cos x), \qquad |x|\leq \arccos (e^ t).  \] Their endpoints join smoothly as a curve, even though those graph charts cease to be regular there. This is an exact implicit formula, rather than a single global graph parametrization. It is recorded in [ BV11 ] , Section 3.1, equation (14), p. 7. Every time slice is a smooth compact embedded strictly convex curve, hence complete and proper, with topology $S^1$ and reflection symmetries across both coordinate axes. It shrinks to the origin at time zero but changes shape and is not a soliton. Its enclosed area is $-2\pi t$, and \[  \kappa _{\max }=(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2},\qquad \kappa _{\min }=e^ t(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2}.  \] The rescaling $(-t)^{-1/2}\Gamma _ t$ converges smoothly to the radius-$\sqrt2$ circle at extinction. As $t\to -\infty $, translating its upper and lower branches to keep their tips fixed gives the two oppositely directed grim-reaper profiles, locally in $|x|<\pi /2$. These limits can be read from the implicit equation: near extinction its quadratic expansion gives $x^2+y^2\sim -2t$, and subtracting the upper tip height gives the limiting graph $\log \cos x$ as $t\to -\infty $. The time slider plots the exact implicit curve for $-5\leq t\leq -0.1$ on a fixed spatial scale.
